newsitem.title: CANADA: Inco still in talks with Sudbury union.
newsitem.headline: Inco still in talks with Sudbury union.

text.p: Inco Ltd continued talks on Thursday with the union representing striking workers at its Sudbury, Ontario nickel mine in hopes of resolving the dispute before a union proposal expired on June 30, sources close to the talks said.
One source said the union and the company were brought together for the talks under a news blackout by Ontario provincial mediator Dennis Nelson, who hoped to broker a deal by the end of the weekend.
"They were talking yesterday. They talked last night and they resumed talking again this morning," the source said. "It's a good sign."

Union sources said this week that the 4,670 striking workers in Sudbury were seeking to improved wages and pensions in a three-year deal ahead of the start of production for Inco's Voisey's Bay, Newfoundland nickel mine, which is expected to begin producing as early as 1999.
"We have to get some of that stuff now before Voisey's Bay starts because after that it's going to be all concessions," a union member said.
Inco spokesman David Allen told Reuters earlier this week that Inco had reserves to supply its customers for about another month.
"We said at the start that we had two months of reserves and it (the strike) hasn't even been a month yet," he said.
But even if the strike was settled in the next few days, Inco had about a three-week maintenance shutdown scheduled to start at the end of June.
Some union sources said that may be why the giant nickel producer was pushing hard for a deal before the scheduled shutdown.
"It would be awful tough for contractors to go in there (during the shutdown) if we're still on strike," one said.

The unionized workers at local 6500 of the United Steelworkers of America, went on strike against Inco at midnight on Monday, June 2, after voting 60.4 percent against a contract offer endorsed by union leaders.
According to Inco's 1997 production plan, the Ontario division was expected to produce about 230 million pounds of nickel, about 200 million pounds of copper and about four million pounds of cobalt.

Inco's Port Colborne, Ontario refinery, which processes cobalt, precious metals and electro-nickel, was not affected by the Sudbury strike. Unionized workers at the refinery approved the contract on Monday, June 2.
